البيروني+ وهي عن السویس. فی 

#وحين كانت أرض مصر بحرآء حرص ملوك الفرس في بعض استيلائهم 
على مصر على أن يحفروا من القلزم (البحر الأحمر) إليهاء ويرفموا البرزخ عما 
ہین البحرین؛ حتى يمكن المركب أن يسير من البحر المحيط في المغرب (المحيط 
الهندي) إليه بالمشرق (الأطلنطي) کل ذلك ارتفاقاً وطلب تعميم المصلحة . وکان

Biruni's Measurement of the Earth
Alberto Gomez Gomez1

Email: agg29@ou.ac.uk,. algomgom@gmail.com

Abstract
The peak from which Biruni measured the Earth is pinpointed; his measurements are shown to tally with the
geographical features of the landscape around the peak. Mathematics shows what measurements he is likely to have
taken, and his famous formula is fully derived. Also, an appendix is given for those who wish to measure mountains
by themselves and follow in Biruni’s footsteps.
Keywords: Biruni, Nandana, Earth’s radius, Baghanwala, Masudic Canon, Hakimite Tables, al-Mamun, Salt Range, Sine Law

1. Introduction
Abu Rayhan (Muhammad ibn Ahmad) al-Biruni
was born in Kath, capital of Khwarezm (the region
of the Amu Darya delta), in modern Khiva, on
September 4, 973 (362-12-03 AH), and died in
Ghazni, Khorasan, on December 13, 1048 (44007-04 AH).1 He was a well-travelled Persian sage
who spoke fluent Persian, Arabic, Turkish, Sanskrit,
Greek, Hebrew, Syrian, and several other local languages in whose literatures he was also well versed.
Not only did he possess ‘all the well known books
on astronomy written within the area extending
from the Mediterranean Sea to the Bay of Bengal, including all the Greek, Indian, and Muslim
authors from Spain to Egypt’ (Biruni, 1956:A13;
Ahmad, 2010:171), but he also wrote prolifically
on all branches of knowledge, like cartography,
geography, ethnography, history, philosophy, mathematics, astronomy, and science in general, a total
of about 180 works, some sadly lost to us now (EI2,
1979:A1237). Chief among these is his Masudic
Canon, an encyclopaedia of astronomy he dedicated
to Sultan Masud, who, delighted with the sage’s
accomplishment, presented him with an elephantload of silver! To everyone’s amazement, Biruni
refused it, pleading that he could not bear to abuse
the generosity of someone who had already shown
him more kindnesses than he felt he deserved (Siraj,
1975:343-4).
1Some think that, according to the solar calendar, the Muslim date
440 AH should be taken to mean AD 1050 (EI2, 1979:A1236, and
Encyclopaedia of World Bibliography, 1973:A578

Of his many contributions to the good of humanity, it is hard to decide which is the most important,
and certainly it is not in the scope of a short paper
like this to do justice to the vastness of his genius.
So, it is as a matter of personal choice that the
author decided to deal here with just one of these:
the fact that he measured the Earth with an unprecedented precision, not equalled in the West until
the 16th century (Norhudzaev, 1973). You may
find the author is rather critical sometimes, for,
in Biruni’s own teachings, it is the truth that we
must seek and speak, even when it goes against
us. His value for the Earth’s radius (6335.725 km)
was the result of having solved a complex geodesic
equation, as we will see. But to fully understand
the whole story, we must know something about its
background and about the early Islamic measures
then (and herein) used: these were exactly those
of ancient Mesopotamia, where ‘each mile was a
third of a farsang, or 4000 cubits, called ‘black’
in Iraq, each of which equalled 24 digits’ (Biruni,
1934:208; Wright, 1934:119; Mercier, 1993:177).
That is, one farsang (5916 m) equalled three miles,
one mile (1972 m) equalled 4000 cubits, and one
(black) cubit (493 mm) equalled twenty-four digits.
Note the connection with the Roman mile (1479 m)
of 3000 cubits (each of 493 mm).

counted.title: European Exploration Innovations: The Role of Afro-Asian Technology and Ideas in European Exploration, 1400–1700
counted.venue: Frontiers in Humanities and Social Sciences
counted.abstract: This paper revisits the formation of the European Age of Exploration by re-examining the claim of an “independent Western breakthrough.” Taking European overseas expansion from 1400 to 1700 as its main thread, the paper argues that Europe’s maritime capabilities did not emerge out of nowhere, but gradually developed through the absorption of mathematical knowledge, astronomical observations, navigational instruments, shipbuilding experience, and gunpowder technologies from Asia and Africa. At the same time, Europe also developed its own distinctive features in its understanding of Atlantic wind systems, the combination of different ship types, and the construction of colonial institutions. By comparing Eurocentric interpretations, the “Great Divergence” theory, and diffusionist explanations, this paper argues that so-called innovation was more fundamentally a process of transforming knowledge across regions. Europe’s rise depended both on the circulation of external knowledge and experience and on the reconfiguration of commercial, military, and colonial power.

3. Borrowed Hardware: The Afro-Asian Origins of European Navigation
and Warfare
3.1.

The Islamic Mathematical Revolution and Astronomical Foundations

European maritime expansion depended not only on ships and navigational instruments but
also on mathematical knowledge accumulated across Afro-Asia. J. Lennart Berggren traces the
decisive transition from the chord-based geometry of the Greeks to the sine-based
trigonometry perfected by medieval Islamic scholars. Ptolemy's Almagest relied on a
cumbersome Table of Chords, the chord being the straight line subtending an arc in a circle of
fixed radius. This system allowed mathematicians to double angles to compute arcs. Islamic
mathematicians adopted the sine function from Indian astronomical texts and translated in the
eighth century. It led to far more elegant and direct calculations [11]. The practical power of
these methods showed in al-Biruni's determination of the Earth's radius from the dip angle of
the horizon observed atop a mountain, and in the qibla problem—the requirement to face
Mecca in prayer—which is a genuine exercise in spherical trigonometry demanding the
latitudes and longitudes of two points on a sphere; solving it repeatedly built exactly the
spherical-triangle techniques that deep-sea navigation would later need [12]. The transmission
of Islamic astronomical knowledge into Europe was not an isolated event but a sustained
process across several centuries. Jabir ibn Aflah's Islah al-Majisti, written in twelfth-century
Seville, was translated from Arabic into Latin in Toledo by Gerard of Cremona in 1175 and later
into Hebrew by Moses ibn Tibbon. It allowed astronomical techniques developed in al-Andalus
to circulate across Christian Europe. Later refinements to planetary tables and solar
observations also entered European scientific practice through multiple channels. The
Gregorian calendar reform adopted measurements of the solar year that were more precise
than those inherited from medieval Latin astronomy, while Arabic astronomical instruments
continued to be adapted by Renaissance craftsmen and studied by European scholars able to
read Arabic. By the fifteenth century, European astronomers and navigators were therefore
working within a scientific tradition that had been substantially enriched through centuries of
Islamic scholarship rather than relying solely on classical Greek inheritance [13]. The practical
impact of this mathematical inheritance is really profound for European development. The sinebased trigonometry perfected by Islamic scholars became the exact mathematics that European
navigators adapted for accurate deep-sea charts and navigation manuals, such as the work of
the Portuguese mathematician Pedro Nunes [14]. When Vasco da Gama's pilots calculated their
139

 Frontiers in Humanities and Social Sciences

Volume 6 Issue 10, 2026

ISSN: 2710-0170

latitude using the altitude of the sun or the Pole Star, they were employing mathematical tools
first developed in 9th-century Baghdad and refined in 12th-century Seville. The European
"Scientific Revolution" of the 16th and 17th centuries was not a rupture with the past but a
continuation and an assimilation—of intellectual traditions that had flourished in the Islamic
world for centuries.

3.2.

Instruments of Celestial Observation: The Astrolabe and Quadrant

Mathematics alone could not navigate a ship. It required instruments to translate theory into
practice and led them to find their way. The most important of these instruments was the
astrolabe, a device that allowed navigators to measure the altitude of celestial bodies and
thereby determine their latitude. While the astrolabe had Greek antecedents, it was Islamic
astronomers who transformed it into a precise, portable, and elegant tool of observation.
Islamic instrument makers developed sophisticated designs, including the universal astrolabe;
unlike standard versions that required different plates for different latitudes, it used a specific
projection that worked at any latitude, making it essential for the global voyages of the Age of
Exploration [15].
The transmission of astrolabe technology to Europe followed the same Iberian routes that
carried Islamic mathematics. Richard Lorch documents the transition of astronomical
instruments to the Iberian Peninsula through figures like Jabir ibn Aflah and the Toledan
translation movement [16]. By the 16th century, European instrument makers were directly
adapting Islamic technology for local use. George Saliba notes that the Arsenius family of
astrolabe makers in the Netherlands fitted Latin star maps (retes) onto Arabic instrument bases
(maters) originally made in Muslim Spain—a literal synthesis of Islamic hardware and
European calibration [17]. The astrolabes carried aboard Portuguese and Spanish exploration
fleets were not European inventions but evolutionary descendants of eleventh-century Toledan
craftsmanship, refined through centuries of Islamic instrument-making before reaching the
hands of Iberian navigators.
The kamal, a simpler but also crucial instrument, was also a direct borrowing from Afro-Asian
navigational technology. It was a simple wooden board strung with a knotted cord and held at
a fixed distance from the eye. It was measured by gripping the knot between the teeth, and the
board let a navigator sight the Pole Star's altitude above the horizon and calculate latitude
without any specialized astronomical training. Vasco da Gama's crew encountered the kamal in
use in the Indian Ocean and immediately recognized its value for exactly this purpose [18]. The
backstaff, which let navigators measure the sun's altitude without looking directly into it, was
a European refinement of an Afro-Asian original — an improvement, not an invention.
Columbus's own journal shows a parallel pattern of practical adaptation to manage his crew's
fear during the long Atlantic crossing; he maintained two separate reckonings of distance and
recorded the first European observation of magnetic variation, noting that the compass needle
pointed not to the North Star itself but to an "invisible fixed point” [19]. Whether or not he
borrowed the knowledge and refined it into new instruments. European celestial navigation at
every level depended on Afro-Asian foundations and did not itself originate.

3.3.

The Compass

If the astrolabe provided a way to measure latitude, the compass provided a way to maintain
direction. The magnetic compass was not a European invention; its origins lie in Han and Song
Dynasty China, where mariners utilized the "south-pointing needle" floated in basins of
seawater to maintain a course during starless nights or foul weather [20]. Chinese sailors had
developed watertight bulkheads, balanced rudders, and sophisticated star-measuring boards
(qianxingban) for determining latitude before any European vessel ventured into t
